name: Child Sexual Abuse Regulation (CSAR, proposal)
evidence_rating: ex-ante only and contested: Commission IA cost forecasts versus critical Parliament complementary IA and regulators' opinion; proposal still in trilogue
summary: The Commission estimated its child sexual abuse proposal would cost online services about EUR 1.5 billion a year and public authorities about EUR 0.8 billion, in exchange for more detection and reporting of abuse. A study for the European Parliament and Europe's data protection authorities found that scanning for new abuse material and grooming is too inaccurate and intrusive to be proportionate. The law was still being negotiated in 2026, so there is no evidence of its effects.

indicators.objective: No LFS indicators were extracted from the proposal's financial statement; the memorandum refers to a monitoring programme in Article 83 and the impact assessment (indicators collected by public authorities, providers and the EU Centre), with evaluation five years after entry into force. The proposal was still in trilogue in mid-2026 (fifth trilogue 29 June 2026); voluntary detection continues under the interim Regulation (EU) 2021/1232, which the Commission proposed to extend to April 2028.
More effective detection, reporting and removal of child sexual abuse online; better victim support
indicators.indicator: Reports of child sexual abuse; removal; victims identified
indicators.target_or_baseline: Qualitative: number of reports expected to increase; reduced fragmentation
indicators.evidence: Not measurable: Regulation not adopted. EPRS complementary IA found tools to detect new material and grooming substantially less accurate than for known material.

indicators.indicator: Costs to providers, public authorities and EU Centre
indicators.target_or_baseline: Providers EUR 1.6bn one-off + EUR 1.5bn/yr; public authorities EUR 5.4m one-off + EUR 825.6m/yr; EU Centre EUR 5m one-off + EUR 25.7m/yr

indicators.objective: Respect for fundamental rights (privacy, data protection)
indicators.target_or_baseline: Safeguards to ensure fair balance and respect prohibition of general monitoring
indicators.evidence: Contested ex ante: EDPB-EDPS and EPRS concluded detection orders risk generalised scanning and would likely fail the proportionality test for new material and grooming.

literature.citation: European Commission (2022), Impact assessment accompanying the proposal laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse (executive summary SWD(2022) 210), SWD(2022) 209
literature.title: Impact assessment accompanying the proposal laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse (executive summary SWD(2022) 210)
literature.outcomes: detection and reporting; costs; fundamental rights
literature.headline: Costs: providers EUR 1.6bn one-off and EUR 1.5bn/yr; public authorities EUR 5.4m one-off and EUR 825.6m/yr; EU Centre EUR 5m one-off and EUR 25.7m/yr; benefits described qualitatively (more reports, less fragmentation, better victim support)
literature.summary_plain: The Commission estimated the rules would cost online services about EUR 1.5 billion a year and public authorities about EUR 0.8 billion a year, in return for more detection and reporting of abuse.
literature.quality: forecast; benefits not monetised in summary

literature.citation: Ecorys, Queen Mary University London et al. for EPRS (2023), Proposal for a regulation laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse: Complementary impact assessment, EPRS study PE 740.248 (requested by LIBE)
literature.authors: Ecorys, Queen Mary University London et al. for EPRS
literature.title: Proposal for a regulation laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse: Complementary impact assessment
literature.method: ex-ante review (legal, technical and cost-benefit analysis)
literature.outcomes: detection accuracy; fundamental rights; EU Centre cost-efficiency
literature.headline: Weaknesses in Commission problem definition (limited treatment of end-to-end encryption); tools for known material accurate, for new material and grooming substantially less accurate; detection orders for new material and grooming would likely fail proportionality test; most cost-efficient EU Centre option is a hybrid with Europol
literature.summary_plain: An independent study for the European Parliament found that scanning for previously unknown abuse images and grooming is too inaccurate and intrusive to be proportionate, and that the Commission underplayed encryption.

literature.citation: EDPB & EDPS (2022), Joint Opinion 04/2022 on the Proposal for a Regulation laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse, EDPB-EDPS Joint Opinion, 28 July 2022
literature.title: Joint Opinion 04/2022 on the Proposal for a Regulation laying down rules to prevent and combat child sexual abuse
literature.outcomes: privacy; data protection; confidentiality of communications
literature.headline: Vague conditions for detection orders risk generalised and indiscriminate scanning; substantial degradation of confidentiality of communications; proposal may present more risks to individuals and society than to criminals pursued
literature.summary_plain: Europe's data protection authorities warned the proposal could lead to indiscriminate scanning of private messages and weaken confidentiality for everyone, children included.
